judgments.reasoning_cat1: The recitals use soft, non-operative language ('approximately 266,200 square feet', 'most advantageous site', 'all factors considered') and a nominal $10.00 recital of consideration, none of which is an operative promise a court would have to apply. The one arguably loaded phrase is 'no-cost assignable option', which is a characterisation rather than a defined term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The recital that Optionee requires a 'no-cost' option sits awkwardly against paragraph 12, which obliges Optionee to use best efforts to reimburse up to $50,000 of traffic-study costs and imposes cooperation burdens, a classic recital-versus-operative-text tension. The mismatch is modest, however, because the recital describes cost to Optionee, not to Optionor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Approximately 10.89 acres' and 'together with all improvements, easements, and appurtenances' leave the exact subject matter to the incorporated Exhibit 1 description, and the closing sentence limits assignability to 'Optionee's developer' while calling the option 'fully assignable at any time'. Those two ideas in one sentence are in mild tension but each is readable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 13 says the Option 'may be assigned by the Optionee, without the consent of the Optionor' with no restriction to a developer, and Exhibit 3 paragraph 1 recites '10.89 acres' without the qualifier 'approximately' — two small but real inconsistencies with this grant. Neither is likely to be outcome-determinative on its own.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'This Option shall continue in effect for a period of not less than one (1) year' fixes only a floor and no expiry, yet the same sentence speaks of exercise 'on or before its expiration' and of a thirty-day extension — the term has no ascertainable end date, which is a genuine, nameable ambiguity ('not less than'). Two parties could reasonably read this as a one-year option or as an option of indefinite duration.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The open-ended term cannot be squared with paragraph 21 (time is of the essence 'throughout the term'), paragraph 14 (termination on failure to exercise 'within the time ... provided herein'), or the thirty-day extension mechanism, all of which presuppose a fixed outside date; Exhibit 3 paragraph 2 repeats the same formula in a recorded instrument. This is the kind of whole-instrument incoherence a court would have to resolve.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause states a $9,000,000 price but pays $8,000,000 at closing and leaves the 'Outstanding Balance' payable only 'at a rate of 10% of the annual tax incremental financing reimbursement received by Developer', with no obligor named, no outside date, and an illustrative 'for example' that may or may not be operative. 'Standard deductions and prorations' and 'less any deductions identified below' are further undefined boundaries.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 4 conditions conveyance on 'payment of the Purchase Price, less the Outstanding Balance', paragraph 8 and paragraph 12 deduct amounts from the Outstanding Balance, and paragraph 12's last sentence says the Outstanding Balance 'shall be retained by Optionee' — yet here the balance flows from TIF received by the Developer, who is not a party. Reconciling who owes and who withholds the balance is genuinely difficult.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The covenant to convey 'good and marketable indefeasible fee simple title ... free and clear of all liens and encumbrances whatsoever' is standard, and the qualifiers ('subject only to ... Permitted Exceptions', 'standard deductions, prorations and or adjustments') are conventional conveyancing language. Nothing in the wording carries two plausible readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This clause defines 'Permitted Exceptions' as the items 'set forth in Exhibit 1', while paragraph 6's second paragraph defines the same capitalised term as those title conditions not objected to or accepted by Optionee — two competing definitions of one defined term in the same instrument. It also conditions conveyance on payment of the Purchase Price 'less the Outstanding Balance', which must be harmonised with paragraph 3.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The obligations are concrete (thirty days, ALTA/ACSM 2005 standards, one tax parcel, certification to the Developer's title company), although 'such Table A items as Optionee may elect' and the placement of 'by December 31, 2006' at the end of a long sentence leave minor uncertainty about what the date attaches to. Overall the drafting is specific and datable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits paragraph 12's street-vacation obligations and the Exhibit 2 attachment list; the December 31, 2006 survey date and the December 1, 2006 Brownfield deadline in paragraph 12 are sequenced sensibly. No operative conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The final sentence switches without explanation to 'Seller' and 'Purchaser', terms defined nowhere in this Option, and duplicates the same thirty-day deadline already stated in the first sentence — a drafting-transplant error. It also promises a policy 'without standard exceptions' and 'free and clear of any liens and encumbrances', which is in tension with the Permitted Exceptions regime.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The unqualified 'free and clear of any liens and encumbrances' here does not sit easily with paragraph 4 and the second paragraph of paragraph 6, both of which contemplate Permitted Exceptions surviving to closing. The undefined Seller/Purchaser labels also require importing Exhibit 1's terminology.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The three enumerated 'options' are grammatically non-parallel ('waiving', 'allow Optionor', 'if the defect can be cured by the payment of dollars, deducting'), and option (3) hands the ultimate choice to Optionor's 'discretion' inside a provision framed as Optionee's option — the reach of Optionee's election is genuinely unclear. 'Unable or unwilling to cure' and 'payment of dollars' are further loose phrases.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its definition of 'Permitted Exceptions' (conditions not objected to or accepted by Optionee) contradicts paragraph 4, which defines the same term as items set forth in Exhibit 1. Option (2) also lets cure attempts run 'during the term of the Option', which interacts with the indefinite term in paragraph 2.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, conventional representation of record ownership and authority with no vague or double-meaning term. Nothing to construe on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with paragraph 22 (Authority of Optionor) and the Exhibit 3 acknowledgement by the Managing Member. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The representation is knowledge-qualified in three different ways ('has no knowledge', 'to its knowledge', 'nor does Optionor know of any facts'), and 'possession ... peaceable and undisturbed' is stated without qualifier, so the scope of the knowledge limitation across the sentence is not perfectly clean. Still, this is familiar representation language.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with paragraph 12, which acknowledges that numerous governmental approvals are still required, and with paragraph 7(d)'s disclosure that the site is a 'facility'; those are disclosures rather than contradictions. No direct conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Of sufficient size, capacity' is a bare adequacy standard with no stated benchmark, and the closing qualifier 'for its current use' may or may not attach to the whole representation — a genuinely ambiguous limitation given the property's contemplated redevelopment. Naming the term is easy: 'sufficient ... capacity ... for its current use'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 12 expressly contemplates 'utility relocation' as one of the required governmental approvals for Optionee's intended use, which sits in some tension with a representation that utilities are available for immediate connection. The tension is softened by the 'current use' qualifier.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The disclosure is anchored to a statutory definition (MCL 324.20101) and to identified environmental reports, which makes it comparatively determinate; 'all environmental information that it has' is broad but self-limiting. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly carved out of the paragraph 7(e) representations and dovetails with paragraph 8's Due Care regime, so the pieces fit. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To the best of Optionor's actual knowledge' combines a best-knowledge and an actual-knowledge standard in one phrase, and the compliance representation sweeps in 'all federal, state and local laws, rules, regulations, ordinances, codes and orders'. The double qualifier is a small, nameable oddity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carve-outs point to Schedule A and paragraph 7(d), both of which exist in the instrument, so the exception structure is coherent. No inconsistency located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Toxic, dangerous or hazardous substances' is a broad triad with no definition, but it is a familiar formula and the temporal anchor ('since the time Optionor acquired any interest') is clear. Modest vagueness only.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is subject to the same Schedule A and paragraph 7(d) carve-outs, and paragraph 7(d)'s admission that the site is a statutory 'facility' due to historic uses is expressly excepted. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The second sentence is garbled — 'The exemptions include that owner's obligations to comply with its due care requirements' inverts exemptions and obligations, and the representation is conditioned on a hypothetical future purchaser availing itself of statutory exemptions. The syntax makes the promised state of affairs hard to pin down.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps with paragraph 8's Due Care allocation and the $500,000 Limitation of Liability, but the two can be read together without contradiction. No specific conflicting provision identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short bring-down covenant; the only soft edge is that it runs 'until and including any exercise of this Option' rather than to closing. That endpoint is stated, not ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Because the representations expire at exercise, they do not run to the closing contemplated by paragraph 9, and paragraph 10 conveys the Property 'as is' — a sequencing gap a purchaser might argue about. Exhibit 1 may fill it, but that document is not before me.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonably cooperate', 'most cost effective and appropriate Due Care activities' and 'best efforts to obtain the maximum allowable reimbursable costs' are three stacked open standards, though each is a familiar commercial formula. 'It is the responsibility of the Optionee to estimate the appropriate costs' is by contrast quite definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It allocates cost estimation to Optionee, which matches paragraph 12's statement that 'Optionee shall determine and supply the list of Eligible Activities'; the residual risk lands on Optionor under the immediately following Limitation of Liability. The pieces are consistent even if the incentives are odd.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The label 'Limitation of Liability' is attached to what is in substance an assumption of liability capped at $500,000, and 'all of the costs and activities necessary to achieve Due Care both during pre and post construction' is an open-ended trigger with no time limit. The mismatch between the label and the operative words is nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A later paragraph 12 provision independently deducts amounts 'up to the Limitation of Liability' from the Outstanding Balance for under-approved Eligible Activity costs, raising a real question whether the two deductions are the same $500,000 or cumulative — and the Outstanding Balance itself is only about $1,000,000 under paragraph 3. That overlap is a genuine internal puzzle.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two short, determinate sentences: ninety days after exercise, at the location in Exhibit 1. Nothing vague.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on 'exercise of this Option', whose timing is governed by the open-ended paragraph 2 term, but the ninety-day measure itself is coherent with paragraphs 4 and 10. No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The second sentence is ungrammatical ('Optionee will have an opportunity to inspect the Property and that the Property will be conveyed in "as is" condition'), leaving unclear whether the inspection right is a condition or a mere recital. The 'as is' conveyance is then qualified by an open cross-reference to two documents.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: An 'as is' conveyance must be reconciled with the substantive paragraph 7 representations and with paragraph 8's allocation of up to $500,000 of unapproved Due Care costs to Optionor; the carve-out 'except as otherwise provided' is what does the reconciling work. That is workable but not free of argument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: After enumerating test borings, plans, surveys and environmental assessments, the clause adds 'any other due diligence matters deemed reasonably prudent' — a catch-all against specifics whose reach is uncertain, and 'subject to the rights, interests, and uses made of the Property by the Optionor' is an undefined limit on the whole right. 'Reasonable notice' is also unquantified.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The entry right runs 'during the period of this Option including any extension periods', which inherits paragraph 2's indefinite term, and it interacts with paragraph 10's inspection sentence. Neither amounts to a squarely conflicting provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A non-exhaustive list ('may include, but not be limited to') of seven approval types is followed by an allocation of expense to Optionor for only two of them (street vacations and zoning variances), leaving the cost and duty for rezoning, site plan approval, special use permits and utility relocation unassigned. That is exactly the general-versus-specific / expressio unius problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The following paragraphs assign the Brownfield Plan work to Optionor and the Eligible Activities list to Optionee, but nothing in the instrument fills the gap for the remaining enumerated approvals; paragraph 12's later 'support and written consent' sentence assumes Optionee will pursue some approvals itself. The silence has to be resolved by reading the whole of paragraph 12 together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'As soon as practical', 'a final determination of those costs' and 'the parties cannot agree to the allocation of those costs' are all undefined triggers for a termination right, and there is no mechanism for declaring a final determination. The termination trigger is therefore hard to date.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It creates a termination right additional to paragraph 14's failure-to-exercise termination, and gives Optionee an exit that must be squared with paragraph 21's time-of-the-essence rule; a court applying the Lovejoy 'comprehensive termination provision' reasoning would have to reconcile the two. The tension is real but secondary.
